beats.text: Ask a chatbot a question, and the answer streams out, one small piece at a time.
Each piece is a token, a word or part of one. They arrive on a steady beat, about one every thirty milliseconds.
That number is what this film is about.
Making one token takes a staggering amount of arithmetic, a hundred and forty billion multiplications and additions.
Yet a modern data-centre chip could get through all of it in about a tenth of a millisecond.
Back at true scale, the arithmetic is just this sliver, under one percent of the thirty milliseconds. More than ninety-nine percent is something else.
The chip isn't slow, and the model behind the chatbot isn't badly written. In one token's time, the chip could do the arithmetic for about three hundred tokens. So what fills the rest?
By the end, you'll work out the thirty milliseconds yourself, from the model's size and two numbers on a chip's specification sheet.
How fast it calculates, and how fast its memory delivers the model. For any model, on any chip.
And the ninety-nine percent has a name.
The memory wall.
A trained model is a file. Open it, and there are no rules, no instructions, no text. Just a very long list of numbers.
Each sits between about minus one and plus one. A large model has seventy billion of them, each called a parameter or, equally, a weight.
Everything that follows is arithmetic on this list. Training produced it, once, over months, on thousands of chips.
Inference is using the list, which never changes again. Each token takes milliseconds, on one chip or a few, every time anyone asks.
Our subject is the second, inference. Almost every confusing claim about cost or speed is about the wrong one of the two.
How were the numbers found? Briefly, since we never train anything here. Still, the word trained should not stay a black box. Hide the next word of real text, and let the model guess.
It guessed sofa. The real word was mat. So nudge every weight a tiny amount, in whichever direction makes that guess better.
Repeat over an enormous amount of text, trillions of tiny nudges. Nobody sets a value by hand, or can say what one weight is for.
Out comes a file of numbers that happens to predict text well. That is all a trained model is.
What does one weight do? One multiplication. An input number, times the weight, gives its contribution to the output. The weight is a dial on how much that input counts.
Feed in a two. At zero, the input is ignored. At one point four four, it dominates. At minus point seven, it pushes the other way.
Training searched for seventy billion settings that make the output useful. The intelligence is in no single dial, but in how they combine.
Five made-up inputs, each multiplied by its own weight. Add the five results to get one value, point eight.
Multiply, then add. That is nearly all the arithmetic a model does. You will meet one of the few extra steps shortly.
A large language model, the kind behind a chatbot, is a stack of layers, each built from this pattern at enormous scale. Later, we count these multiplies and adds.
Remember the tokens from the very start? Text is cut into these pieces. Here, five words make five tokens.
Common words are one token. Rarer ones split into two or three. Five hundred words of English make about six to eight hundred tokens.
The model never sees letters, only these pieces, and it produces them one at a time.
Tokens are the unit everything is counted in. Tokens per second. Cost per token. Milliseconds per token.
A model does not write a sentence. The text so far goes in, the whole model runs, and one new token comes out.
It is appended, and the whole model runs again from the start. This is the generate loop.
So a five-hundred-token answer, a few hundred words, means running the whole seventy-billion-parameter model five hundred times.
This loop is the shape of the entire problem. Almost everything difficult about inference comes from repeating the whole model for every token.
What comes out of one turn? Say the text reads, curled up asleep on the sofa was a, then a blank. The model scores every token it knows.
Cat, eight point two. Dog, seven point one. The little word the, three point five. Banana, point four.
And so on, through its whole vocabulary of about a hundred and twenty-eight thousand tokens. Higher means a better fit. These raw scores are called logits.
The values are illustrative, but the shape is real. One or two stand out, and the rest trail off to nothing.
A very common misconception is that a model picks a word. It produces a hundred and twenty-eight thousand numbers, and something else picks.
Is eight point two a lot? Better to have shares of one whole. The scores were made up, but this arithmetic is real.
Step one, the exponential. Raise the number e, about two point seven one eight, to the power of each score. Eight point two becomes about three thousand six hundred and forty-one.

Even negative scores give positive results, and a share cannot be negative. Step two. Divide each by the total, about four thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight. Cat gets seventy-four point five percent, dog twenty-four point eight, the other two under one percent.
With just these four, the shares add to exactly one. This recipe, softmax, is one of those extra steps. It is why a model's output is called a probability.
Each point of score gap multiplies the odds by about two point seven. Cat leads dog by one point one, so it is three times as likely.
The little word the, four point seven behind, gets that multiplier once per point: a hundred and ten times less likely. The exponential exaggerates every gap.
Who picks, then? Not the model. It gives the same shares every time it sees this text.
A token is drawn at random, in proportion to those shares, like a spinner with slices sized to match. This draw is called sampling.
Spin once, and cat is likely. Spin again, and dog can win, about one time in four. If dog is appended, the answer takes a different turn.
So the same question can get different answers, with nothing in the model changed. It all lies in the last step, the draw.
One turn of the generate loop, draw included, takes about thirty milliseconds, three hundredths of a second.
That is about thirty-three tokens a second, words arriving at least as fast as you read.
That is the target, and not an arbitrary one: comfortably faster than anyone reads.
Soon you will derive it from the model's size and a chip's specification sheet.
File sizes are counted in bytes, and each weight takes two. So seventy billion weights make a hundred and forty billion bytes, a hundred and forty gigabytes.
It lives in three places. A disk stores it. The memory beside the chip holds it while the model runs. The chip itself, which does the arithmetic, holds almost nothing.
A few hundred thousand bytes in each small working area, a tenth of a gigabyte in all.
Reading it all off a fast disk takes about twenty seconds. From the memory beside the chip, tens of milliseconds.
So the model is loaded once, at start-up, and stays put. The disk plays no part in making tokens. This film lives in the memory beside the chip.
Picture the model's working life: a load of many seconds, then a token every thirty milliseconds, for hours.
The load is real, but paid once. Shared among a day's millions of tokens, it is about seven millionths of a second each.
A fixed cost stops mattering once spread over enough work. That is amortising, and it comes back often. Next comes a cost that, one token at a time, refuses to spread.
Here is that cost. Each token needs all seventy billion weights, which the chip cannot keep. So for one conversation, every token streams all hundred and forty gigabytes in from memory.
Time per token is the bytes to read, divided by the bytes the memory delivers each second, its bandwidth. Hence the name, high bandwidth memory, H B M.
Bandwidth is one of those two specification numbers. The other, how fast the chip calculates, does not even appear.
The memory on Nvidia's H one hundred delivers three point three five terabytes a second, a terabyte being a thousand gigabytes. So each token takes forty-one point eight milliseconds.
The H two hundred takes twenty-nine point two. There are your thirty milliseconds, right on target. The B two hundred, seventeen point five.
Not a guess, not a benchmark: a division, the best the chip can do, and it moves with model size and memory speed.
Later you will meet about twenty-four tokens a second, not thirty-three. A clash? One second divided by forty-one point eight milliseconds is twenty-three point nine, the H one hundred row.
Same division, different chip. Running down clashes like that is a habit worth having.
On the left, a trained checkpoint, the saved weights. On the right, a service that responds, a token every thirty milliseconds.
Training made the checkpoint. Turning it into something a person can talk to, at a price that works, is its own discipline.
Why does the reading, not the arithmetic, hold the gap between them at thirty milliseconds, not far less? That is the rest of this film. Everything between those two boxes is inference.
A service like that does not run on your laptop. Your question crosses the network to a server, and the answer comes back.
Your laptop has one small chip. The server has a few G P Us, big chips built for this work, and never switches off.
It sits in a data centre, a warehouse of servers, powered and cooled day and night. Almost everything ahead happens inside one server, in a fraction of a second.
Shared by many, always on, and paid for by the hour. That is production.
Your request passes through five pieces of software, each solving a different problem. A router picks the machine. A scheduler batches it with other people's requests, to run together.
A memory manager decides which weights go in which chip's memory. Kernels, small programs on the chip, do the arithmetic. Orchestration wires it all together.
Only one of the five does arithmetic. The other four exist because arithmetic is not the hard part. This series shows why each exists.
Why does this stack matter? Follow the money. About two thirds of all computing power for artificial intelligence now goes to inference.
Big cloud companies are spending around seven hundred billion dollars on A I this year. One provider alone serves over twenty trillion tokens a day.
At that scale, every decision, from chip layout to memory tiers to scheduling, collapses into one number. Cost per token.
Inference overtaking training is a recent inversion. These numbers are uncertain estimates; the direction is not. Serving is where the money now goes.
The traffic is not one user waiting politely, but thousands of conversations at unpredictable moments, all needing the same machines.
That crowd makes the economics work. Run together, each conversation costs less, and much of this film explains why.
But one slow request in a batch holds back everyone's next token. Averages hide rare delays, so the measurements near the film's end judge the worst case.
Add one word to production: concurrent. Shared, concurrent, and paid for, unlike running a model once on your own machine.
One request carries the conversation so far, the new question, and settings, like how random the draw should be.
The surprise: the whole conversation is re-sent every time, because the model remembers nothing between requests. That is called stateless.
Counting only the conversation, with twenty-token questions and two-hundred-token answers, turn two sends two hundred and forty tokens, and turn ten two thousand, to ask a twenty-token question.
So a long conversation means a long input every turn. Length becomes a hardware problem, not bookkeeping, and later explains a growing cost.
Services also put their own text first, the system prompt, where whoever runs them says how the assistant should behave.
But the weights, all hundred and forty gigabytes, are the same for everyone, forever, finished before that text existed. None of it is in the model.
So whatever shapes the answer must be in the context, the tokens in front of the model on that run. No other channel exists, no cupboard to reach into.
Everything hangs on this. The context window, all the model can take in at once, is its only input.
Two questions get confused. Does the system prompt reach the context? Yes, every turn, as do tool definitions and any loaded skill, coming next. The architecture forces it.
Does it cross the network from your device? That varies. It is a product decision about storage.

Three places. Your device, like a developer's system prompt, sent with every call. The server, for you, like project files or custom instructions. Or the server, one copy for everyone, like the provider's prompt.

All three are glued into one prompt, in a fixed order: most shared first, then yours, the conversation, your newest message. A developer's prompt or the provider's: same destination, same cost. Only the storage varies.
The order matters. The model remembers nothing, but the server may briefly keep a running record of work done on text it has seen. The next chapter shows what.
It reuses that work only for a beginning identical token for token, called a prefix. Most shared first makes the prefix longest. Newest first, and nothing matches.
A tool is something the model can ask to have done. Its description, its name, inputs and output, is text in the context. Its code never is.
The model cannot execute anything. It emits text shaped like a call, the serving system spots it, ordinary software runs the code, and the result returns as text.
The code can live anywhere, even in a plugin, a bundle of tools. The model never sees a line, only enough description to call it.
A long description costs tokens every turn. A thousand lines of code cost none. That makes tools affordable: the expensive part is documentation, not behaviour.
A skill is a packet of instructions for one kind of job. Only a catalogue is always present: a name and a sentence each, about thirty tokens.
When your request matches one, its full instructions load, about two thousand tokens. The rest stay one-liners.
Forty skills make a twelve-hundred-token catalogue, affordable. All forty in full would be eighty thousand, forty percent of a large window, before you type.
Load only the one you need: twelve hundred plus two thousand is thirty-two hundred, twenty-five times less. Plugins work the same way.
That is progressive disclosure, forced by arithmetic: every skill fully loaded would cost more of the window than the conversation.
Now total the preamble, everything in front of your first word: the provider's prompt, tool definitions, your custom instructions, one loaded skill.
Four thousand seven hundred and fifty tokens, before any catalogue, nearly two hundred and forty times a twenty-token question.
None of it is in your message, yet every turn it counts against your window, and you pay for reading it in, then looking back over it for each answer token.
These figures are illustrative; the shape is not. Storage is invisible to you. Token count is not, and the preamble is almost always the largest thing in the request.
Press send, and your words cross to a server, maybe an ocean away. The model runs once per token. Is your text re-sent for every token, or the answer shipped once finished? Neither.
One request goes up, once, carrying the prompt. A new example: a weather chat's follow-up, whose whole prompt is one thousand and thirty-two tokens.
The line stays open, and the answer comes down one token at a time, each in a small frame, as it is made.
Nothing more goes up; your device only listens. One journey up, many small journeys down, one open connection. That is streaming, on the wire.
You can check this. Text arrives steadily, not in one lump. And pressing stop halfway works: the rest is never computed.
A non-streaming mode, for programs, sends the whole answer at once: same generation, different delivery. Chat windows stream so the first word shows in under a second.
Neither check would work if the answer were assembled first and sent afterwards. Tokens leave as they are made.
Why not a round trip per token, out and back? Making a token takes thirty milliseconds; a round trip across one city, five. Seoul to Tokyo, thirty-five.
Seoul to the American west coast, a hundred and thirty, over four tokens' worth. Typical figures, not measured ones.
Over that route, a five-hundred-token answer streams in fifteen seconds. A round trip per token makes each a hundred and sixty milliseconds: eighty seconds, sixty-five of them waiting.
Making the token is the quick part; asking for it across an ocean is not. Nearer routes suffer less, but none is free, so the line is opened once, and held.
Follow one token. The instant it is made, it goes onto the open line. Sixty-five milliseconds later, half that west-coast round trip, it is on your screen.
To any human, that is one moment. Nothing waits for the answer to finish.
Now a token every thirty milliseconds. Every trip is the same length, so you read at exactly the pace the model writes.
So the trip only delays the first word, by tens of milliseconds. Reading your prompt in takes hundreds.
Held back until finished, the answer would show nothing for fifteen seconds, then all at once. That, you would notice.
A constant delay shifts a stream without stretching it, so it feels smooth from across the world.
Is the network at least busy? Count bytes, about a letter each. One turn sends at most four kilobytes up, then nothing, and twenty-two kilobytes down.
Inside the machine, every token reads all a hundred and forty gigabytes of weights. Five hundred tokens, with the machine to yourself, read seventy terabytes from memory.
On an H two hundred, at four point eight terabytes per second, that is about fifteen seconds, the fifteen you watched.
Twenty-two kilobytes against seventy terabytes is over three billion to one, a millimetre against over three thousand kilometres. Blaming the network for a slow answer is almost always wrong.
On the server, each new token goes three places. First, down the line to you. That is all the stream showed.
Second, into the cache: a running record the server keeps of everything it has already processed, the kept work promised earlier.
Each token adds two bundles of numbers, its keys and values, explained later. Think of them as notes, kept so they need not be redone during this answer.
Third, the token becomes the next input, which is what autoregressive means. So making the answer, called decode, cannot produce several of your tokens at once. Your token nine needs token eight.
The loop runs until a stop token, meaning done, or a length limit. Each turn, the cache grows by one entry. The server feeds itself while it feeds you.
That record untangles two things called re-sending. Within one answer, nothing is re-sent. The server holds the state, its notes on the conversation so far, in its cache.
Between turns, everything is. Your next message is a new request carrying the whole conversation, because officially the server is stateless, as you saw.
Its notes may survive, making the repeat cheap to process, but the text still travels, every turn.
Per token, nothing repeats, and it costs nothing. Per turn, everything does, and it all counts again. Almost every misunderstanding here comes from mixing the two.
Now one token, end to end: the router and scheduler you met earlier, then prefill, reading your prompt in and making its notes.
In large systems, another machine writes the answer, so a K V transfer hands it those notes, the keys and values. Decode runs that loop, streaming each token to your screen.
Each box has its own problem and fix; most later videos in this series improve one of them. A map worth returning to.
Underneath all six sits one question, which the rest of this film answers. A token takes about thirty milliseconds. Where, exactly, does that time go?
First suspect, the arithmetic. You heard it takes about a tenth of a millisecond. Time to check, by counting operations.
An operation is one piece of arithmetic. One multiplication or one addition, on two numbers. Not a line of code, nor a step of reasoning.
Its proper name is a floating-point operation, or flop. Floating point means numbers with a fractional part, like the weights. Counting them measures a job, the way metres measure distance.
A flop is deliberately tiny. Soon one token will cost a hundred and forty billion of exactly these.
Numbers that big need a shorthand. Ten to the three is a one followed by three zeros, a thousand. The small raised number, the exponent, counts the zeros.
Then a million, a billion, a trillion, and ten to the fifteen, a quadrillion, a thousand million million. Each step is a thousand times the last.
On an ordinary scale, the quadrillion fills the width and the rest vanish. Let each bar count zeros instead, a logarithmic scale, and all five fit.

The whole argument compares two numbers like these. A chip does about ten to the fifteen operations a second. A token needs about ten to the eleven. Four powers of ten apart, a factor of ten thousand.
Ten to the eleven is a count, how many operations a job needs, with no time in it. Ten to the fifteen a second is a rate, with time built in.
Yet they are written almost the same. Flop for the count, flops for the rate.
Confusing the two is the most common mistake in this subject, and checking the units catches it.
Divide a count by a rate, like distance by speed, and you get a time. That one division is the entire calculation ahead.
First, the count. Each token uses all seventy billion weights, each multiplied once and added once. Two operations per weight make a hundred and forty billion, about ten to the eleven.
Now divide. A second holds a thousand milliseconds, so a quadrillion a second is a trillion every millisecond. A token needs a tenth of that, so a tenth of a millisecond.
Yet each token takes thirty milliseconds, its whole budget. The arithmetic comes in tiny bursts, spread across all thirty. Squeezed together, it would fill zero point one milliseconds.
That leaves twenty-nine point nine milliseconds, room for three hundred more tokens' worth. So the film's one question sharpens. Why is that time not free?
Back to that division, the heart of the puzzle. Slowly, this time. Ten to the eleven is eleven tens multiplied together, one per zero. Ten to the fifteen is fifteen of them.
Each ten on top cancels one below. Eleven pairs go, and four tens stay on the bottom. So dividing powers of ten means subtracting the exponents.
Eleven minus fifteen is minus four. So, ten to the minus four. A negative exponent means a fraction, one ten-thousandth of a second, or a tenth of a millisecond.
The units cancel too. Operations, top and bottom, go. Per second means divided by a second. Divide by that, and the second flips back to the top. Seconds are left, as a duration should be.
Multiply instead, and you get operations squared per second. Not a duration, not anything. Something is wrong.
This five-second check catches most errors in this subject. Use it on every claim from here on, including the ones made here.
Now the gap as a ratio. Thirty milliseconds over zero point one is three hundred. The budget is three hundred times the arithmetic.
On one scale, the arithmetic is the sliver from the very start. On arithmetic alone, the chip could make three hundred tokens in the time it takes to make one.
In words, a ratio is easy to nod along to. Drawn to scale, it is hard to shrug off.
Turn the ratio upside down. Zero point one over thirty is about zero point zero zero three three. As a percentage, a fraction out of a hundred, that is a third of one percent.

Unrounded, the arithmetic takes about a seventh of a millisecond. Nearer half a percent, and about two hundred times, not three hundred. The exact figure depends on the model and the chip. The power of ten does not.
Two ways of saying one thing, because a ratio and a percentage land differently on different people.
Here is where the thirty milliseconds goes. Under one percent of it is mathematics. The other ninety-nine percent is something else.
Remember, the chip is not slow, nor the model badly written. There is a clue. The thirty milliseconds came from dividing bytes by memory speed.
This coral part already has a name, the memory wall. Next chapter shows what fills it. Later, two numbers off the chip's specification sheet will explain the whole gap, for any model on any chip.
This bar is the thesis of the whole film. Every idea from here on is an attempt to shrink the coral part.
What fills the coral ninety-nine percent? Start with the chip.
A laptop's processor, a C P U, is a few fast workers, each clever and quick to switch tasks.
A graphics processing unit, a G P U, is thousands of slow, plain ones, all doing the same thing at once to different numbers.
A token is about seventy billion multiplications, in huge groups where none waits on another, so a G P U clears thousands at a time.
The graphics in its name is historical: colouring pixels is the same shape of work. Its weakness is chains, each step needing the last, like writing one token at a time.
Not chosen for cleverness, then, but because the workload is a vast number of identical, independent multiplications, the one thing it's good at.
The chip itself is the G P U's compute die, one piece of silicon that calculates. It holds only about a thousandth of the model.
The memory beside it, separate silicon, holds all seventy billion weights and does no arithmetic. A bus, a bundle of wires, joins them.
So every weight crosses that bus, every token. That's the coral ninety-nine percent: moving the weights, and waiting for them.
Were they in one place, there'd be no memory wall, and no need for this series.
What crosses is bits, single yes-or-no signals, each a voltage on a wire. Ten voltage levels could hold a digit, but telling ten apart, billions of times a second, on a warm chip, is far too hard.

Two levels, called one and zero, tolerate noise: a one can sag a long way and still read correctly. So every number is built from them, for engineering reasons, not mathematical ones, and counted in bits.
Eight bits make a byte, and a weight takes two, enough for useful accuracy. That's why seventy billion weights make the hundred and forty gigabytes.
Sixteen bits is the usual choice. Shrinking it comes later in the series. Parameters times bytes gives bytes. You'll use that constantly.
Bits cross at a rate, the bandwidth from earlier. It's not speed in the everyday sense, but width times frequency: how many wires, times how often each sends a bit.
A laptop's memory is a narrow pipe running fast. Not much gets through, about a hundred gigabytes a second.
The H one hundred's is a wide pipe running steadily: five thousand one hundred and twenty wires, each a little slower, for three point three five terabytes per second.
Memory gets faster mostly by getting wider, and that many wires can't be long, so it sits against the chip.
Why not put the memory on the chip? Each chip is optimised for one job. Logic and dense storage need different manufacturing processes, and nobody has made both work well on one piece of silicon.
And there isn't room. A hundred and forty gigabytes won't fit on a postage stamp of silicon, at any price.
So the memory sits off the chip, as close as possible, across the widest bus that can be built. Close is not the same as on, and that difference is the memory wall.
It's not an oversight anyone could have avoided. It follows from what silicon can and cannot do.
Every request the chip sends to memory makes a trip. How long one takes, from ask to arrive, is latency. Bandwidth is how much travels at once.
They're independent. A container ship takes weeks, carrying a town's goods. A second doubles the goods, not the weeks. A motorbike courier is the reverse.
Memory can't be made low-latency: distance and physics are what they are. But enough requests in flight keep the pipe from running dry.
Confusing the two produces many of the wrong intuitions in this field. Hold them apart.
A rate is an amount divided by a time: bytes per second, where per does the dividing. So a rate times a time gives back an amount.
Give the H one hundred our thirty milliseconds, the faster H two hundred's figure. Three point three five terabytes a second, times thirty milliseconds, is about a hundred gigabytes.
Not the hundred and forty needed: the whole story in one line of arithmetic. The earlier division says it from the other side: forty-two milliseconds, not thirty.
Every specification is an amount or a rate, and keeping them apart is most of the skill. Take the H one hundred's sheet.

Memory capacity, eighty gigabytes: an amount. Bandwidth: a rate. Peak compute, nine hundred and eighty-nine teraflops, tera meaning trillion: a rate. Power, seven hundred watts, energy per second: a rate too.
On a sheet, the commonest slip is mistaking capacity for bandwidth: count and rate again. Capacity says whether the model fits. Bandwidth says how fast it's read once it does. A chip can fail either.
Ours fails the first: a hundred and forty gigabytes won't fit in eighty, so it needs two chips. Every number ahead comes off a sheet like this, and telling amount from rate sorts most claims.
Two lines matter most: compute throughput, operations per second, and memory bandwidth, bytes per second. A token needs both: fetch the weights, and multiply them.
Pretend the model fits on one H one hundred. Unrounded, a token's arithmetic takes about a seventh of a millisecond. Reading the weights, forty-two milliseconds.

They overlap: while one slice of weights is multiplied, the next is fetched. The slower one sets the pace, leaving the other idle, here the arithmetic. Forty-two milliseconds, not an average of twenty-one.
Two independent resources. Almost every performance question from here on asks which one a workload runs out of first.
They also grow at different speeds. Transistors are the tiny switches arithmetic is built from, and compute scales with how densely they're packed. No hard ceiling yet.
Bandwidth is a product of three. The memory comes in stacks, towers of layers, wired to the chip through pins: rate per pin, times pins per stack, times stacks.
The H one hundred's five stacks of one thousand and twenty-four pins are the five thousand one hundred and twenty wires from earlier.
Each term has a ceiling. Pins switch only so fast before high and low blur. Only so many connections fit under a stack. And the package holding the stacks has edges. So memory is hard to speed up.
Compute keeps climbing. Bandwidth fights three ceilings set by geometry and physics, not lack of effort. That's the memory wall's mechanism: one lever against three.
Across one decade of top-tier server G P Us, on a log axis where each step multiplies, compute rose about eighty times.
Off-chip bandwidth rose about seventeen times. Eighty over seventeen is about four point seven.
The curves are schematic, the endpoints real, and still spreading. One decade moved the balance by almost a factor of five.
Two computer architects, Wulf and McKee, named the memory wall in nineteen ninety-five, more than twenty years before the transformer, the design behind today's language models.
What changed is the workload, not the hardware trend. The gap was always there. Now a computation hungry enough for bytes makes it the dominant concern.
Language-model inference is among the most byte-hungry workloads ever built.
That's the memory wall: arithmetic waiting on memory, because the two live apart and the gap between their speeds keeps growing.
Not an A I problem hardware failed to anticipate, but a long-standing trend A I walked straight into.
Every decision in production inference, and every paper in this series, takes one line as given. If you remember one thing, make it this. The rest is working out what it implies.
Arithmetic is cheap. Data movement is expensive.
To see what actually moves, two words first. A vector is a list of numbers, like these eight. A matrix is a grid of them, four rows of eight.
That's all the linear algebra you need. A vector stands for one token. A matrix holds a block of weights.
A model is a few hundred such grids. Running it means multiplying vectors by them: multiply and add, almost nothing else.
Take five inputs and a matrix, four rows of five. Lay the first row along them and multiply each pair.
Add the products, and that single number, zero point five, is the output's first entry.
Every row does the same, filling the output vector: the multiply-and-add from the very start.
Twenty weights mean twenty multiplications and twenty additions. Each weight is used exactly once, the fact every operation count rests on.
Scaled up, it's the only heavy operation in the model. Everything else is a rounding error beside it.
But you type text. The tokeniser first cuts it into the tokens you met earlier, on average a little smaller than words.
Then the embedding step turns each token into a vector, eight thousand one hundred and ninety-two numbers long in our model.
Neither conversion is a calculation. Both are lookups. From here on there's no text, only numbers, and everything downstream is linear algebra.
The embedding table has a row for every token the model knows, about a hundred and twenty-eight thousand.
The tokeniser turns fox into a whole number, its token I D, say four thousand two hundred and seventy-one. It isn't fed into a formula. It's a row number: the model copies that row out.
No arithmetic touches the weights, no multiplication, no addition. Just one memory read, at the row's address. That's a lookup.
The table is learned like any other weights, but reaching into it costs zero floating-point operations.
Textbooks write this as a multiply: a one-hot vector, all zeros except a single one at fox's row, times the table, gives fox's row.
Unlike the input before, this one is as long as the table is tall, so it stands down the side. Each output number takes a column of pairs, all but one times zero, and zero adds nothing.
True, but nobody does it: about a billion multiplications to copy one row. The maths says multiply. The hardware does a gather, fetching rows from memory.
Multiply and gather cost different things, operations against memory reads, which matters from here on. A habit worth keeping: several steps are written as a multiply and done as something cheaper.
At the model's other end, a table of the same shape, the output projection, scores every token.
On the way in, a two-hundred-token prompt reads two hundred rows, zero point one six percent. The rest is never touched.
On the way out, the model reads every row, all two point one gigabytes, again for every new token.
Zero operations in. Out, one multiply and one add per weight, two point one billion operations, from a table exactly the same size.
Some models use one table for both ends. Ours keeps two. Either way, one end gathers a few rows, the other streams them all.
A genuine exception to the rule that every token reads every weight: one of the largest matrices adds almost no traffic on the way in.
These vectors still lack one thing. The dog bit the man. The man bit the dog. Identical tokens, entirely different meaning.
The lookup gives dog the same row wherever it sits, so both sentences become the same bag of vectors, and would get the same answer.
Each token must also carry where it sits. Position is added into each vector at the start, or applied inside attention, where tokens look at each other, which comes next.
Our model does the second. Easy to state, easy to forget: the vectors alone don't say what order anything came in.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: The vectors now enter the stack of layers. Each layer does two things. First, attention moves information between tokens, the only place one token's vector can change another's.
Then the feed-forward network transforms each vector alone. Nearly every optimisation later treats these two steps separately.
A layer gives back one vector per token, just as wide, but better, carrying more of what the surrounding text implies.

Same shape out as in, so each layer's output feeds the next. That makes depth, the number of layers, possible. Ours has eighty, each with its own weights: eighty rounds of the same kind of refinement.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: Attention rests on one idea, the weighted average. A plain average of ten, twenty and thirty is twenty, each counting equally.
Now weight them: ten by a half, twenty by point three, thirty by point two. Five plus six plus six makes seventeen.
The weights add to one, so the answer stays between ten and thirty, pulled towards ten, which counts for half.
Change only the weights and the answer moves, with no value changed. What the values are, how much each counts: attention is that separation.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: Inside attention, each token's vector is multiplied by three weight matrices: W Q, W K and W V, for query, key and value. Out come three vectors, with position worked into query and key.
The query: what this token is looking for. The key: what it offers others. The value: what it contributes when matched. These very keys and values are kept in the cache, the server's running record.
Comparing every query with every key, by the same multiply and add, scores how well each pair matches: a grid, a row per token asking, a column per token asked.
A token looks only back, never ahead. The scores blend the values into an updated vector for each position. That is how context crosses between tokens.
With thousands of tokens the grid grows enormous: the central object of the third video.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: Now run the weighted average on tokens. After the cat sat down comes a new word, it. Its query meets the four earlier keys.
Suppose the word the scores zero, cat two point five, sat one point seven, down zero, leaving out the new word's own score.
Softmax, from earlier, turns these into shares: point oh five, point six two, point two eight, point oh five. Together, one.
They blend the four values: sixty-two percent cat, five percent the word the. The new word now carries mostly cat.
Attention is a weighted average over the tokens so far: the query asks, the keys set the shares, the values get averaged. These shares are illustrative; adding to one is not.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: Meaning depends on what came before. Bank after river is not bank after savings, because attention blends in a different neighbour.
Context, met earlier, is everything the model can see: the whole prompt so far plus the newest token. Each new token looks at all of it.
Context length, the window's size, is how many tokens attention can look across. Past it, the earliest fall out and can influence nothing.
A long conversation is not just a longer input, but more work per token. Context length is not only a storage limit: it is a recurring cost.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: Here is a natural picture: multiply each embedding by W Q, W K and W V once, then carry the three results up every layer.
Everything so far invites it: fixed weights, an embedding looked up once. Why multiply twice?
But it is not what happens. Each layer owns its own three matrices: eighty of each kind, learned separately, all different.
So the multiply happens eighty times per token, each against a different matrix and a different input. Layer forty's W K has nothing to do with layer thirty-nine's.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: What travels up the stack is one vector per token, as wide as the embedding: the residual stream.
Each layer reads the stream, makes a fresh query, key and value, uses and discards them, then adds its result back on. Hence the name, residual.
Keys and values are the one partial exception: kept for the cache, each layer keeping its own.
Only layer one makes them straight from the embedding. Higher up, the stream has already mixed in earlier tokens, so a key depends on everything before it. That later decides what can be reused.
The residual stream is the only thing that flows. Everything else is made and used up within one layer.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: In one layer, attention has four weight matrices: query, key, value, and combine, written W O, which turns the blended result into the stream's update.
The classic feed-forward has two, one widening each vector, one narrowing it back: six per layer. Ours adds a gate, a second widening matrix deciding how much of each widened number passes: seven.
Across eighty layers, that is five hundred and sixty, none shared. So the parameter count grows in direct proportion to depth, and every token reads all of them.
Eighty rounds of the same kind of step, but not the same work: eighty different sets of weights to fetch.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: The strongest evidence for per-layer matrices: add up the sizes, using a published model's real shapes.
W Q maps the stream's eight thousand one hundred and ninety-two numbers to a query just as wide. Square that: sixty-seven point one million weights.
Attention runs as sixty-four small attentions, called heads, each a hundred and twenty-eight numbers wide. Keys and values get only eight heads, each shared by eight query heads.
So W K and W V are an eighth as wide, eight point four million each, a saving that pays off with the cache. W O matches W Q. Attention, per layer: a hundred and fifty-one million.
The feed-forward widens each vector three and a half times, so its three matrices hold seven hundred and four point six million.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: One layer: eight hundred and fifty-five point six million. Times eighty, sixty-eight point five billion.
Add the two vocabulary tables: the embedding, one point oh five billion weights, and a separate, same-sized output projection, or output head. Two point one billion in all.
Total, seventy point six billion, against an advertised seventy. It lands, within rounding.
Suppose W Q, W K and W V existed once for the whole model. Seventy-nine of eighty copies vanish, six point six billion weights, leaving just under sixty-four billion: over six billion short.
So per-layer matrices are not a design opinion. They are the only version that adds up.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: So what does depth buy? After one layer, a token knows its neighbours. After ten, its phrase. After forty, its sentence. After eighty, the whole passage.
That is intuition, not measurement. What is certain: each layer builds only on the one below.
The cost, though, is exact: linear in depth. Eighty layers, eighty times the weights and the reading, every token. The next chapter's byte count rests on that.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

beats.text: Last step. The top layer gives out vectors, not words, and only the last position's vector is needed.
It is multiplied by the output projection, the embedding's twin, read in full every token: about a hundred and twenty-eight thousand scores. Softmax makes shares, and one token is drawn.

Embedding lookup, eighty layers, output projection, pick one: that trip is a forward pass. The pick is appended and the next pass begins, closing the loop from the very start. Everything between is arithmetic on arrays of numbers.

Seven matrices a layer, six in the classic design, times sixty to over a hundred layers: these learned weights are the model. Everything else divides by their count and size, or multiplies against them.

chapter.title: Layers, attention, and the parameter count
chapter.kicker: 08 · Layers, attention, and the parameter count

chapter.title: The weights, and what they cost to move
chapter.kicker: 09 · The weights, and what they cost to move

beats.text: You have met this conversion: seventy billion parameters, at two bytes each, make a hundred and forty gigabytes.
That is the entire model, off the chip in the memory beside it, the same for every request.

One last look at the disk. From a fast drive, fetching it all takes about twenty seconds, twenty thousand milliseconds. From the memory beside an H one hundred, if it fitted, about forty-two milliseconds: roughly five hundred times faster.
And from the chip itself? Not slow, but impossible. It holds about a tenth of a gigabyte in all.
That's why the model is loaded once, and stays. Disk speeds vary widely, but the gap stays enormous. The disk explains only slow start-ups, and why nobody streams weights from storage.

chapter.title: The weights, and what they cost to move
chapter.kicker: 09 · The weights, and what they cost to move

beats.text: Here is the package, carrying chip and memory together. At its centre, the chip itself: the compute die, one piece of silicon.
Around it, the stacks: memory dies, bonded one on another. The H one hundred has five, eighty gigabytes in all.
Why call it high bandwidth memory, H B M? Not because each wire is faster. It sits millimetres away on the same package, joined by those five thousand one hundred and twenty wires: close, and wide.
As you saw, wide needs short. Thousands of wires must be hair-thin, and thin wires carry a clean signal only over millimetres, so the memory cannot move further out and grow.
The name describes a placement, not a technology. The price is memory that is small and expensive.

chapter.title: The weights, and what they cost to move
chapter.kicker: 09 · The weights, and what they cost to move

beats.text: While the service runs, the weights are only read, never written: copied out, never changed. Training rewrote them at every step. Serving leaves them exactly as they were.
Two users, two questions, the same hundred and forty gigabytes doing both jobs. So one copy serves everybody, which later makes batching possible: many users per pass.
The other side: every forward pass moves all one hundred and forty gigabytes across that bus, into the arithmetic units.
That is pure overhead, paid again and again. Nothing is learned, or saved, by having fetched the weights before.

Two consequences, pointing opposite ways. One copy serves everyone, yet the same bytes are fetched every single time. The memory is close, but close is not the same as on, and every token pays for that trip.

chapter.title: The weights, and what they cost to move
chapter.kicker: 09 · The weights, and what they cost to move

beats.text: Every forward pass makes that trip. A request's passes come in two very different phases.
First, prefill, reading the prompt in. Eight tokens climb the eighty layers together, in parallel.
It ends with an updated vector at every position, and the first answer token.
Then decode: each new token pays for its own full trip through the model, again and again, until a stop token or length limit.
Same chip, same weights, same code. What differs is how many tokens share each load of the weights.
Why can only prefill run in parallel? Timing. Every prompt token is known up front, so nothing waits.
You met this earlier: in decode, no token exists until the one before it is chosen. A chain.
A G P U's thousands of workers can share out independent work, never a chain, however many sit idle. That one distinction drives every difference.
Earlier, each weight cost two operations, a multiply and an add. Exact, or a rule of thumb?
Back to the row-by-row multiply: a four-by-six matrix and one token's six inputs. Row one's output is weight one times input one, plus weight two times input two, and so on.
Each term is one instruction, a multiply-accumulate, counted as two operations for its two results, a product and a new total. That is the only source of the two.
Every weight lands in exactly one term of one output. Not once per layer or per head. Once. Twenty-four weights, forty-eight operations: twice the cells, for any shape.
Exact, then, not a rule of thumb: with one input vector, no weight is used twice in a token's pass.
Every matrix in every layer obeys this: query, key, value and combine, then the feed-forward's two, or three in ours.
Add them all, plus the embedding table and output projection: operations per token are twice the parameter count.
The rule holds matrix by matrix, so it survives the sum: the one number every model advertises prices a forward pass on its own.
Every rule has a boundary. Attention scores the newest query against every key, then blends the values by the shares.
Queries, keys, values and shares are made on the fly from your tokens: activations, not weights. That is real work the rule never counts.

So this cost grows with the context's length, not the model's size. Per earlier token, sixty-four heads each score and blend a hundred and twenty-eight numbers, two operations apiece, in eighty layers: about two point six million operations.

Against the weights' hundred and forty billion, about two thousand tokens of context add four percent, a rounding error. At eight thousand tokens, fifteen percent. At a hundred and twenty-eight thousand tokens, two hundred and forty percent, and the rule stops being useful.

Two smaller corrections. The embedding table, one and a half percent of the parameters, is counted, yet a lookup multiplies nothing: an overcount. Softmax and normalisation, small rescaling steps, add a little back.
So the rule prices the weights, and they are the whole story only while the context is short.
Run the rule on our model. Seventy billion parameters, times two: a hundred and forty billion operations per token. The bytes: the same count times two bytes, a hundred and forty gigabytes.
One parameter count gives both, worth knowing by heart. The two twos are unrelated, one from the multiply-accumulate, one from sixteen bits.
So, counting the weights, a one-token decode step does exactly one operation per byte. That ratio is called arithmetic intensity.
Divide the H one hundred's compute rate by its bandwidth: while one byte arrives, it could do about two hundred and ninety-five operations. Decode offers one.
At best, a third of one percent of the arithmetic is busy: under one percent, as the thirty-millisecond puzzle found.
In decode, one token means one input vector: each weight arrives, does one multiply-accumulate, and is done. In a two-thousand-token prefill, it does two thousand.
The bus pays the same toll in both phases, a hundred and forty gigabytes. Prefill's payoff is thousands of times larger.
Is decode slow because the model is large? True, but beside the point: what changes is the work each byte does.

Amortising, which you met with the start-up load and will meet constantly, means spreading a fixed cost over more work. It is just division: a hundred and forty gigabytes over the tokens sharing the read.
One token carries it all. Ten carry fourteen gigabytes each. Two thousand tokens, seventy megabytes each. The read never changes; the share falls in exact proportion.
Prefill sits at the bottom; decode, one token per read, is stuck at the top. The structural fact of inference: one request's decode has nobody to share the cost with.
Decode's one operation per byte holds only at sixteen bits. At thirty-two bits, the bytes double: half an operation per byte.
Eight-bit integers give two per byte, four-bit, four. The operations never move. Storing weights in fewer bits, called quantization, only shrinks the bytes.
Batching, many users' tokens sharing each read, multiplies operations per byte by the number sharing.

At sixteen bits, reaching the chip's two hundred and ninety-five operations per byte takes two hundred and ninety-five tokens per read. Thirty-two-bit weights need twice as many, eight-bit half, four-bit a quarter.

That balance point is the next chapter's ridge. The payoff of the whole derivation: one rule for operations, one for bytes, and their ratio decides whether a chip waits on maths or memory. For one user's decode, it is one.
Picture a laundry: washing takes thirty minutes a load, drying an hour, folding ten, all at once. A load leaves once an hour.
Faster washing or folding changes nothing. The slowest step, the bottleneck, sets the pace; only improving it helps.
A chip has the two stations you met earlier: memory delivering bytes, arithmetic using them. A workload is bound by whichever it runs out of first.
Memory bound, like decode: the arithmetic idles, waiting for data. Compute bound: the memory has bandwidth to spare. Both are wasteful, in different ways.
Except at one balance point, only one limit binds, so the picture ahead has two regions.
One ratio, set against one number from the chip, predicts which bound a workload hits, before you run anything. Last chapter named it: arithmetic intensity, operations performed over bytes moved.
It's the work done per byte dragged in from off-chip memory. High intensity reuses each byte many times. Low intensity loads a byte, does almost nothing, needs another.
Decode's, as you found, is one: two operations per two-byte weight, from the shapes alone. That ratio is the single most useful number in this story.
Put one, three, thirty and three hundred on an ordinary scale running to ten thousand. Small things vanish: three hundred a stub, thirty a hairline, three and one gone.
On the logarithmic scale from earlier, each step means ten times, not plus ten. So three, thirty and three hundred sit evenly spaced.
Both axes ahead work this way, the only way to see one and three hundred together. On them, a straight line means multiplying, not adding.
A point is a pair of numbers. Down to the bottom axis for one: intensity. Across to the side for the other: how fast a workload runs.
Each workload is one point: its left-right place from the workload, its ceiling from the chip. Enough to read the shape ahead, not take it on trust.
Now, logarithmic axes. On an H one hundred, arithmetic sets a flat ceiling, the peak: nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion operations a second, however much work each byte brings.
Memory sets a slanted one, bandwidth times intensity. At one operation per byte, three point three five trillion bytes a second feed as many operations a second. At ten, ten times that.
A multiplication, so on these axes, a straight line. Faster memory only lifts it.
No workload passes either ceiling, so its attainable speed is the minimum: the peak, or bandwidth times intensity.
At ten operations per byte, that's memory's thirty-three and a half trillion. At a thousand, the peak.
Keep the lower line everywhere, and a roof appears. No convention to memorise: just two independent limits, and the lower one always wins.
Left of the corner, memory bound: more work per byte, more speed. Right, compute bound: the arithmetic units are already full, and improving the bytes buys nothing.

The corner, where the limits are equal, is the ridge. That's the entire diagram: the roofline, from Williams, Waterman and Patterson, two thousand nine. Two ceilings, one rule for choosing between them.
What sets the corner? Two toy chips. One does five hundred operations and reads fifty bytes a second; the other, twice both. Operations over bytes: ten for both.
Both corners sit at that ratio, ten operations per byte, so a workload lands on the same side on both: at five, memory bound; at twenty, compute bound.
The ratio says what work a chip suits; the absolute numbers, how fast. Two different questions.
The memory wall is about this ratio. Over the decade you saw, compute grew about eighty times, bandwidth seventeen, pushing the corner about four point seven times right.
A ratio is scale-free, so it suits a trend held across many hardware generations.
The ridge is where bandwidth times intensity equals the peak, so intensity equals peak over bandwidth, the toy chips' ratio. Two spec-sheet numbers, no workload: a property of the chip alone.
On an H one hundred, nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion over three point three five trillion: two hundred and ninety-five operations per byte, last chapter's number.
Below it, memory bound. Above it, compute bound. One division, and the chip is characterised. Do it once for your own hardware: it's what every workload gets compared against.

The roofline assumes three things. One memory level, ignoring the cache hierarchy: small, fast stores near the arithmetic, like the working areas. Not the server's cache, the running record: same word, different job.
No launch latency, though real work takes a moment to start. Perfect pipelining, every station always busy, though real chips have bubbles, idle gaps.
So the roof is a best case: real workloads land on it or below, never above.
A simplification on every count. Yet as a first check of whether a workload starves the arithmetic or the memory bus, it has held since two thousand nine.
Knowing its assumptions lets you trust it where it applies, and distrust it where it doesn't.

Operations per byte, phase by phase. Prefill first: two thousand prompt tokens at a hundred and forty billion operations each, two hundred and eighty trillion. Attention adds a few percent, about two hundred and ninety trillion.
Yet the weights cross the bus once, a hundred and forty gigabytes, plus about six for activations and the running record. About two thousand operations per byte.
Decode, one request's next token: a hundred and forty billion operations, on the same hundred and forty gigabytes every time. The chip itself holds only about a tenth of a gigabyte.
Same model, same chip, both from the shapes alone: two thousand against one. Decode gets one operation from each identical byte.
On the roofline, prefill sits about seven times right of the ridge: arithmetic flat out, bandwidth to spare.
Decode sits nearly three hundred times left, low on the slanted ceiling: bus almost always busy, arithmetic under one percent.
That's where the ninety-nine percent went. Nothing is broken: the workload's shape leaves the chip able only to wait.
Two points, two thousand times apart. Almost everything ahead tries to move the left one rightward.

Decode's top speed is bandwidth over bytes per token: the thirty-millisecond division, flipped. On an H one hundred, pretending the model fits, three point three five terabytes a second over a hundred and forty gigabytes: about twenty-four tokens a second.
A physical ceiling, not a software one: no cleverer kernel beats it, since even instant arithmetic waits for bytes.
It bounds every serving system on this chip, with sixteen-bit weights and one token per read: the most one answer can stream, and the most the chip can make.
Only three ways past it, one per condition. Raise bandwidth: a different chip. Or shrink the bytes: eight-bit weights give about forty-eight a second.

Or amortise each read: ten batched requests make about two hundred and forty a second, counting the weights alone, each still at twenty-four. A later trick amortises within one answer: guess ahead, then check several tokens in one read.
Each gets its own video. One line of arithmetic, three escape routes: the entire roadmap.
Each decode step reads every weight. It also reads the conversation so far, and that grows.
Each row is one decode step. Its newest token attends to every earlier token and itself: four, then five, then six. That staircase is the picture behind a cost growing with the square of the length.
The model keeps no memory between steps. So its work on earlier tokens is redone every time, or kept, in a store that grows. Which is cheaper?
Back to the grid of scores. Token one sees only itself. Token five sees all five.
Everything ahead is masked out: the causal mask. A token sees only what came before it, so only a triangle is used.
You met the chain earlier: no token exists until the one before is chosen. Under the mask, each new row only looks back, never changing those above.
Prefill, with every token present, fills the triangle in one shot. Decode adds a row at a time.
That chain is in the work itself, not the hardware. This triangle is the whole reason the two phases differ.
The observation that saves everything: earlier keys and values do not depend on the new token. Settled when their tokens were processed, they never change.
Recomputing them repeats identical work. Generating token one thousand would recompute all nine hundred and ninety-nine earlier positions.
Add it up. Multiply the length by one less than itself, then halve it. For a thousand, about half a million recomputations, where a thousand would do.

Two shapes worth recognising. Linear: flat work per token. Quadratic: each token costs more than the last. At ten tokens, under five times apart. At ten thousand, quadratic is five thousand times worse.
Recomputing is the quadratic shape, so nobody does it: long conversations would be impossible, not merely expensive. Almost every scaling problem ahead is one such term outgrowing everything linear.
The general idea first: it makes the specific easier to judge. A cache is something kept so it need not be made again.
Work it out once, note it, then read the note. The trade is always memory for time, paying only if the note is read again.
In decode, every earlier token is needed at every later step, about as favourable as it gets. The cost: the store grows every token. That is the key-value cache.
The running record from earlier is exactly this: every token's keys and values, in a dedicated region of H B M.
Each decode step now computes only the new token's key and value, appends them, and reads the whole cache for attention.
Nothing earlier is recomputed: each key and value is made once, so that work goes from quadratic to linear. Every serving system does this; it is why decode is practical at all.
But every token still reads the whole cache: the staircase from the start, each step reading more than the last.
A caching trick that solves one problem and creates the one that dominates everything downstream: why so many optimisations ahead exist.
One correction to the loop as first drawn. Do all one thousand and thirty-two tokens of the weather chat re-enter the model every step?
That would be a thousand times the work at this length, and worse as it grows. Only the newest token goes through. The rest is already there, as keys and values.
The sequence grows, but the work per step does not grow with it the way that picture suggests.
How big is the cache? Build its formula for one token: two, one key and one value, then the layers.
In the natural picture from earlier, query, key and value are made once and carried up: no layers term. But every layer makes its own, from its own input and weights.
All eighty are kept: layer forty needs an earlier token's layer-forty key, not its layer-one key. Made once, the cache would be eighty times smaller, and much of this series would not exist.
The rest is our model's shape: eight key-value heads, each a hundred and twenty-eight numbers wide, two bytes per number.
Two, times eight, times a hundred and twenty-eight, times two: four thousand and ninety-six bytes per layer. Times eighty: three hundred and twenty-seven thousand, six hundred and eighty bytes.
Three hundred and twenty kilobytes per token, counting a kilobyte as one thousand and twenty-four bytes. It is large because all eighty layers hold their own version of the token.
Now the shared key-value heads pay off. Sixty-four, one per query head, would make the cache eight times bigger: about two point six megabytes per token.
That eightfold cut is grouped-query attention, already built in. Nothing cuts the layers, because they are the model.
So every technique that shrinks the cache attacks another term: fewer heads, narrower heads, or fewer bytes per number. Knowing which makes the series ahead easier to follow.
The cache grows in a straight line with the conversation. A thousand tokens: a third of a gigabyte. Ten thousand: three point three gigabytes.
A hundred thousand: thirty-three gigabytes, already about a quarter of the model itself, for one conversation.
A formula worth memorising: it turns any model's shape and context length straight into gigabytes.
Every step reads every weight and every cache entry so far, over one bus. So the ceiling from earlier, bandwidth over bytes per token, sinks as the cache grows.

On our what-if H one hundred, weights alone allow about twenty-four tokens a second. Add a hundred-thousand-token cache, and each step reads a hundred and seventy-three gigabytes: about nineteen. Illustrative, but the direction is general.
Batching shares one read of the weights among many conversations, but each cache is read for one conversation alone.

So the model and each conversation's state compete, which shapes every technique ahead: shrinking the cache, sharing it between requests that start alike, splitting it across machines, or never storing parts at all.
Two different things, reading from one budget. Once the cache is large, optimising the weights alone stops being enough.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: Recall that a token's key depends on the tokens before it, at almost every layer. Yet a key is just the token's vector, times the key matrix, W K.
Each layer's W K is fixed once training ends, the same for every token, position, conversation and user, forever. So the matrix itself really is independent of context.
Which makes this a fair question. If the matrix is fixed, how can the key depend on earlier tokens?
The answer is in what gets multiplied. A fixed function of a changing input is a changing output.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: At layer one, position five's key starts from token five's own embedding row, and position is worked in as the key is made.
Nothing there depends on tokens one to four. Change token two, and that input stays bit for bit identical. The fixed-matrix reasoning is exactly right.

Token five's layer-one key and value could sit in a table, correct in any sentence. A one-layer model would need no prefix rule, the rule from earlier that reuse stops at the first changed token. Same I D, same position: reusable, whatever came before.
So grant it fully: the independence is real. It survives exactly one layer.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: In layer one, attention at position five blends all five tokens' values into a weighted average. With stand-in values, ten to fifty, the blend is thirty-three. Change token two's value to sixty, and the blend becomes forty-five.
Through the combine step, that blend is added into position five's residual stream. So what layer one hands upward carries every token before it.
That is not a side effect. It is the purpose of a layer, to make each vector reflect its context.
Layer one: same input, same key. Layer two's W K, the same for both sentences, gets a different vector and makes a different key. You cannot have context-aware vectors and context-free keys.
And it compounds, eighty times over. The dependence enters through the residual stream, never the weights. They learn nothing about your sentence. The vector arriving at them already knows.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: To check, a tiny four-layer transformer, with causal attention, feed-forward blocks and residual connections, was run twice, with only token two changed.
At each layer, token five's two keys were compared number by number and rolled into one distance. Zero means every number matched.
Layer one: zero, to the last bit. Layer two: about three point five. Layer three: sixteen point seven. Layer four: twenty point one, growing as the mixing compounds, in this run.
The weights were random, so the sizes mean nothing. The pattern is the point: layer one identical, every layer above it moved.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: The same fact, from the other side. Take bank again: the river bank, and the savings bank. Same token, same position, same W K.
Their layer-one keys match. Above that, the vectors going into W K differ, one blended with river, one with savings. One key leans toward water, the other toward money.
That is how the model tells them apart. Keys blind to context all the way up could not, and the model would be useless.
So the question and the capability are one phenomenon, and that dependence is exactly what makes the prefix rule necessary.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: When token two changes, could the cache keep layer one's keys and values, and throw away the rest? In principle, yes, for the unchanged tokens.
In practice, layer one is a rounding error: one point two five percent of the prefill work. The other ninety-eight point seven five percent is all recomputed.

And the saving is smaller still. Layer two needs layer one's output, so layer one's attention runs anyway. Only its key and value multiplications are skipped: about a fortieth of one percent of the arithmetic.
So serving systems stick to the prefix rule, right for layers two and up. Layer one's entries are still valid, but one layer in eighty is not worth an exception, or the bookkeeping.

chapter.title: Why a key depends on its context
chapter.kicker: 14 · Why a key depends on its context

beats.text: The K V cache has two jobs. During an answer, it grows: each new token appends its keys and values, and nothing is searched for.
When your next message arrives, the cache is searched, once. The server asks: do I already hold keys and values for the beginning of this prompt?
Where it does, those tokens skip prefill: a cache hit, what people call a warm cache. This reuse is prompt caching.
Where it holds no match, it is a miss, and those tokens are prefilled. Only the search can hit or miss.
The cache holds neither text nor answers. Your words sit in a database, away from the model's server, and travel with every turn.
It holds what the model made from them: for each token, a key and a value in each of eighty layers, which later tokens attend to. The token's processed form, in its context.
Take the weather chat: four kilobytes of text, but a third of a gigabyte of keys and values, over eighty thousand times more. Making them is exactly what prefill does.
So a hit does not save sending the text, which is cheap. It saves remaking keys and values, the expensive part the cache is for.

Earlier you saw keys and values are settled once made, because attention is causal. Above layer one, token five's keys and values come from tokens one to four, and itself. Nothing later can reach back.
That is the whole permission for caching. A value that could still change is unsafe to keep. A settled one is safe, while there is room.
A kept value stays valid while its token, and every one before it, is unchanged. Causality has now done three things: it made decode one at a time, halved the score grid, and here makes caching safe.

Back to the earlier case: a prompt arrives with token two changed. Token three is unchanged, but its keys and values were made in a context holding the old token two. They are now wrong, as are those of four to seven.

The match cannot skip a difference and resume. Everything from the first mismatch is recomputed, identical or not. A prefix rule, not a search for pieces. Not a design choice: it follows from what keys and values are.
Now a real request: system prompt, tools, history, your new message. Below, what the server holds. The match runs from the front, and stops at the first difference.

The weather chat's prompt was itself a follow-up: one thousand and twenty-seven of its one thousand and thirty-two tokens match. Only your five new ones are prefilled: a hit rate of ninety-nine point five percent.
Nearly all of it is text you never wrote: the system prompt, the tools, the model's own answers.
That front-to-back rule explains every warm and cold case to come.
The server holds the question, What is the capital of France? The new prompt says, Tell me the capital of France please.
Four words are shared: capital, of, France, and the little word the, even in the same positions. But compare from the front: What against Tell. The match never begins.

Everything shared sits behind that difference, worthless however much there is. A hit needs the sequence identical from the beginning, in order. It is the commonest misunderstanding about prompt caching.
In short. Shared vocabulary counts for nothing. Only a shared beginning counts.
The whole rule, in one line. Compare from token one, and stop at the first difference. Before it, a hit, reused. After it, a miss, prefilled.
The useful question is never how similar, but how identical, and from where. Diverge only at the very end, and almost everything hits. Differ in the first word, and nothing does.
Order matters as much as content. Remember how a prompt is ordered: most shared first, then yours, the conversation, your newest message. This rule is why.
The next chapter is this one sentence, applied case by case.
Warm and cold are counts, not moods. A minute later, the weather conversation's follow-up brought one thousand and thirty-two tokens, all but five already cached. That is warm.
A day later, in the coldest case, nothing is cached: all one thousand and thirty-two are prefilled, two hundred and six times the work.

The only difference is the cache, stored in fixed-size blocks, each holding keys and values for a few tokens. Warm, yours are still resident in the G P U's memory. Cold, they were evicted for someone else.
Only the small text survives, in the database away from the model's server. Your keys and values stopped existing, and prefill must rebuild every one from that text.
So warm is a precise question. How many arriving tokens already have keys and values on this machine?
Now a smaller example, counted token by token. A service starts every conversation with the same preamble, system prompt and tools, seven hundred and seventy tokens.
At time t you ask, What is the capital of France? Seven tokens. Nothing in the cache matches, so all seven hundred and seventy-seven are prefilled.
The cold case, unavoidable the first time. Yet on a busy machine the preamble is probably cached already, leaving your seven tokens the only new work.
Case A: you continue the chat. The model answered, The capital of France is Paris. A minute later you add four new tokens. And its population?
That answer was cached as it was written, so everything before your new words matches. Hit, seven hundred and eighty-four. Prefill, four.
A perfect prefix, the model's own answer included. The best and most common case, and why a conversation stays quick while you keep typing.
Case B, a minute later, a new conversation: What is the capital of Japan? The preamble and the first five words match, identical and in the same places.
Then France meets Japan, and the match ends. The question mark after it is redone too. Hit, seven hundred and seventy-five. Prefill, two.
A partial hit mid-sentence, which you could not arrange. Same-shaped questions start alike, and the rule never asks whose conversation, only whether tokens are identical from the front.
Case C, the pair from earlier: Tell me the capital of France, please. It shares the whole phrase, the capital of France, but the very first token differs.
Only the shared preamble hits, seven hundred and seventy. All seven of your tokens are prefilled. Your words contributed nothing.
B and C are both seven tokens, like the original, sharing many of its words. Yet B matches five, C none, decided by which word came first.
Against the whole prompt, all three hits look excellent, ninety-nine point one percent or better, because the preamble dominates and always matches.
Count only your seven tokens. In case A, all seven matched, plus the whole history. Only four new tokens were fresh. B, five of seven. C, none.
Same hits, opposite stories, decided by where the first divergence falls. The whole-prompt number flatters and hides the part you control, yet it is the one usually reported.
Why is a minute warm and a day cold? The cache is not a private locker but a fixed pool on one machine, and everyone competes for it.
When a new request needs room, the least recently used blocks, untouched the longest, are dropped. Nothing is on a timer. It is pure pressure.
A minute later, your blocks may survive on a quiet machine and be gone on a busy one. A day later, other people's conversations have flushed them everywhere.

Providers quote a lifetime of a few minutes, a guideline about typical load, not a guarantee. Eviction follows demand for space, not time: warmth is likely, not certain, and fades rather than expires.
Now send case A's follow-up a day later. Your history was evicted overnight, so prefill rebuilds it from text.
The preamble is different: the most shared text in the system. Its keys and values are computed once per machine and reused by every request.
Touched by thousands of conversations all day, it is almost never least recently used: the most reliable hit there is. Hit, seven hundred and seventy. Prefill, eighteen, against four a minute later.
That only helps on the same machine, so the router sends each request where its prefix already sits.
The preamble usually survives, kept warm because it is shared. Yours does not, because nobody else was keeping it alive.
Warmth also makes a large fixed preamble cheap. A cached read, an input token already held, skips prefill, so it is cheap to serve. Providers price it at roughly a tenth of a fresh one.
Illustratively, case C's seven hundred and seventy-seven input tokens would bill like about eighty-four fresh ones.
The preamble's warmth is not luck. It comes from being shared, and it is why cached input is priced separately.
Being shared also makes the preamble expensive to edit. Change one token at position five, and the match ends there. Nothing after it is reused, however identical.
Every conversation on the machine shares that prefix, so all go cold at once. The weather conversation's next turn prefills one thousand and twenty-eight tokens, not five.
About two hundred and six times the prefill work, from one token. So operators edit a production system prompt with care.
Most stable text first, most variable last: the ordering you met earlier. It keeps everyday changes away from the front everyone shares.
