What about the person waiting? Take the mail: latency, how long one letter takes; throughput, how many arrive per day.
A van filling all week has enormous throughput and terrible latency. A courier, off with each letter, is the reverse.
Neither is better. Unlike memory's latency and bandwidth, these often pull against each other.
Nothing here needed a computer, yet a serving system faces this choice: wait to gather requests and do more, or answer at once and do less.
But the first request waits for the rest. Soon, only tokens arriving in time will count.
Press send, and you feel two waits. The pause before the first word: time to first token. Each gap after it: time per output token.

Prefill makes the pause: the whole prompt passes through every layer before any output. Half a second for a short prompt, several seconds for a long one. Real chips run below full speed; queues add more.
Decode makes each gap: every token needs its own complete forward pass.
The pause decides whether a product feels responsive; the gaps, whether text reads comfortably or stutters, breaking concentration. Both are felt, made at opposite ends of the roofline.
A cache hit skips prefill for every matched token. Warm, the weather conversation prefilled five, not one thousand and thirty-two.
Two hundred and six times less work, yet here only three and a half times less waiting: one read of the weights remains.
Decode is untouched: every token still reads all one hundred and forty gigabytes. Making a token never depended on how the context was assembled.
So caching is purely a prefill optimisation. Of the two waits you feel, it shortens only the first.
Caching is often said to make the model faster. It makes it start sooner, then stream at the same speed.
Different bottlenecks, different engineering. For a long prompt, time to first token is a compute problem: keep the arithmetic units fed.

Time per output token is a bandwidth problem: move fewer bytes per token. Swap the H one hundred for an H two hundred: same arithmetic, faster memory. The gaps shrink to our thirty milliseconds; the pause barely moves.
A change can even hurt the other. Prefill each new prompt on arrival, for a quicker first word, and streaming answers can stall.
That is why serving systems eventually split the two phases onto different hardware.
Throughput is every token generated per second. Goodput filters it down to tokens delivered inside the promised latency targets, judged per request: averages hide rare delays.
Pack thousands of requests into huge, slow batches: the counter looks impressive. But if every user stares at a blank screen for forty seconds, every token missed its target. Goodput is zero.
Tokens nobody was willing to wait for. Goodput is throughput times the share that arrived in time.
Goodput, not raw throughput, is what production systems optimise. For anyone who operates a system rather than benchmarks one, no distinction matters more.
Thirty milliseconds a token, and a tenth of one for its arithmetic. That gap is not a mystery. It is a division.
Two hardware numbers, peak arithmetic over bandwidth, make the chip's ridge. Divide by one property of the workload, decode's one operation per byte, and that is the gap.

Two hundred and ninety-five on an H one hundred. On the H two hundred behind the thirty milliseconds, same arithmetic speed, faster memory, just over two hundred. Three hundred came from round numbers.

Five sentences explain the thirty milliseconds. Compute outgrows bandwidth, eighty times against seventeen in a decade, so the ridge climbs. A forward pass streams every weight, a hundred and forty gigabytes a token.
Prefill amortises that read, decode does not: every token pays it in full. The K V cache adds to the bill, three hundred and twenty kilobytes per token held.
And goodput, the tokens that arrive in time, is what is actually sold. Each link is a division or a multiplication you can now do yourself, nothing beyond arithmetic.

For decode, flip the thirty-millisecond division: tokens per second is bandwidth over bytes per token. Bytes per token is bytes per read over the tokens sharing it. Those three terms are the escape routes from earlier.
Ahead: inside the G P U, and the code on it. Fewer bits per weight. One model across many chips.
Models using only part of themselves per token. Serving at scale. Decode's idle arithmetic, put to work. And one real request, traced end to end through the whole stack.
Each attacks that division, most by moving one term. Hold that frame, and the series reads as a single argument.
Arithmetic is cheap. Data movement is expensive.
Next, inside the G P U. This has been The Memory Wall.
